clue.text: Arrogant position of Pegasus

explanation.surface: A description of the winged horse of myth striking a haughty pose.
explanation.walkthrough: Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth, flies high, so it is literally a horse up high; the phrase also names the superior attitude of someone who looks down on others.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on one's high horse is an idiom for a haughty, superior stance; Pegasus is a flying steed, a horse aloft.

clue.text: Like families at play

parts.note: the card game in which players collect sets of four family members is named for contented families

explanation.surface: How families seem when playing together.
explanation.walkthrough: Happy Families is a traditional British children's card game, so families in play are named by the game's adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The card game's title calls its families cheerful, which also describes contented families having fun.

clue.text: Light green vehicles ?

parts.note: a green traffic light means go
carts are simple wheeled vehicles

explanation.surface: Small eco-friendly cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light green' looks like a colour, but it is the traffic signal meaning go; the whole clue also describes the lightweight racing vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Small, light motor vehicles for racing on tracks are karts, earlier spelt with a C.

clue.text: Capital tie-up

parts.note: capital is read as the head, and a tie-up is a cloth knotted around it

explanation.surface: A financial merger or a traffic jam in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' suggests money or a city, but it means the head, from Latin caput; the 'tie-up' is a square of cloth knotted over it.
explanation.definitionFit: A square of cloth worn tied over the hair is fastened around the head.

clue.text: Put in again, pulled up about the Horse's Rest

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for pulled up goes round the horse's rest

parts.note: reined means pulled up, as a rider checks a horse with the reins
a stall is a compartment in a stable where a horse rests

explanation.surface: A horse brought back to its stable after being pulled up.
explanation.definitionFit: Installing something a second time means fitting it in place again.

clue.text: Go astray in strange territory

indicators.note: in tells us the letters lie inside the following words

explanation.surface: Wander off in unknown lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange territory' looks like a setting, but its second word holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To err originally meant to wander, and now means to make a mistake or stray from the right course.

clue.text: Eastern ruler's away up North, in New Brunswick

indicators.note: in tells us the Scots word goes inside the province's abbreviation

parts.note: NB is the standard abbreviation for the Canadian province of New Brunswick
awa is the Scots form of away, so it is how the word is said up north in Scotland

explanation.surface: A tale of an Oriental prince who has gone off northwards to a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up North' looks like a direction or a reversal signal, but it marks the Scottish form of 'away'. The 's after ruler stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nawab was a Muslim governor or prince in Mughal India, an Eastern potentate.

clue.text: A biblical mother-in-law raises one complaint

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something means reading it from bottom to top, so the whole run turns round

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a moan is a complaint

explanation.surface: A woman from scripture voices a grievance about her son's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raises' reverses I MOAN in this down clue. Naomi is Ruth's mother-in-law in the Book of Ruth.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Ruth, the Moabite Ruth stays loyal to her husband's mother after both are widowed.

clue.text: Nondescript bit of furniture

explanation.surface: A dull, ordinary piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a noun: a thing hard to name.
explanation.definitionFit: A word for some unspecified item or thingummy; also a stand with open shelves for ornaments.

clue.text: Sarah's whoop at the whist-table ?

parts.note: Sarah Battle is the whist-loving old lady of Charles Lamb's essay Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist, and her shout is named after her

explanation.surface: A woman cries out in triumph at a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb's essay about Mrs Sarah Battle, who took whist with deadly seriousness, lets her surname plus 'cry' make a war shout.
explanation.definitionFit: A shout raised by troops charging into combat is a war cry.

clue.text: Napierian confession of error ?

parts.note: General Sir Charles Napier is said to have reported his capture of Sind in 1843 with a one-word Latin message meaning 'I have sinned'

explanation.surface: A general's admission that he got something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The story is that Napier punned on Sind and 'sinned' by sending the Latin for 'I have sinned'; the word is still used for any admission of guilt.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for 'I have sinned' serves in English as a formal acknowledgement of wrongdoing.

clue.text: Brazilian diplomacy, we read, to keep the peace

definitions.text: we read, to keep the peace

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is the famous Brazilian city, so Brazilian gives Rio
tact is the diplomacy of saying the right thing

explanation.surface: South American statesmanship, it is reported, keeps things calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we read' looks like a sound signal, but it belongs to the definition: the Riot Act is what authorities read aloud to a crowd to disperse it and keep the peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the 1714 statute, magistrates read a proclamation ordering a crowd to disperse; reading it became the standard step against a disorderly assembly.

clue.text: Stories that are woven

explanation.surface: Tales told on a loom.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are linked: a story is 'spun' like thread, and spun thread is what a weaver weaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall tales are called yarns, and spun threads woven into cloth are yarns too.

clue.text: Built up of parts-Celia's not involved

indicators.note: involved means twisted or tangled, so the letters are mixed up together

parts.note: the possessive s counts as a letter here, giving the six letters of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something assembled from components, though Celia had no part in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not involved' reads as Celia staying out, but 'not' is fodder and 'involved' the anagram signal: CELIAS plus NOT rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sectional furniture or buildings are made in separate units that fit together.

clue.text: The producer has the last word

definitions.text: The producer has the last word

parts.words: The producer has the last word
parts.note: a theatrical producer chooses actors, and a deciding ballot in a tie is the final say

explanation.surface: In the theatre, the director decides.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a producer choosing the cast, but the phrase means the deciding ballot a chairman gives when votes are tied.
explanation.definitionFit: When a vote is tied, the chair's extra ballot settles the matter, so it is the decisive word.

clue.text: Bumble's law

parts.note: Mr Bumble, the beadle in Dickens's Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: A legal principle named after its discoverer, Bumble.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a scientific rule (Boyle's law, Murphy's law), but it refers to Mr Bumble's famous verdict on the law in Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's beadle calls the law a donkey, meaning a fool, when told he is responsible for his wife's actions.

clue.text: What one who enjoys poor health feels for this malady ?

definitions.text: What one who enjoys poor health feels for this malady ?

parts.words: What one who enjoys poor health feels for this malady ?
parts.note: the word means both fondness and, in older usage, a disease, so a hypochondriac feels fondness for the illness itself

explanation.surface: A hypochondriac's feelings about his illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enjoys poor health' is an idiom for a hypochondriac; such a person feels fondness for an illness, and the same word once meant a disease.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means warm fondness and is also an old medical term for a morbid condition of the body.

clue.text: A number in hospital

parts.note: number is read as 'something that numbs', a drug used in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: A patient, or a figure, at the infirmary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' suggests a figure or a patient's ward number, but it means a thing that makes numb.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons use drugs that remove sensation, numbing the patient before an operation.

clue.text: Like a nightmare at " the witching time of night "?

definitions.text: Like a nightmare at " the witching time of night "?

parts.words: Like a nightmare at " the witching time of night "?
parts.note: the quotation is Hamlet's, and at midnight witches were said to ride sleepers, causing bad dreams

explanation.surface: Describing a bad dream at midnight, in Hamlet's words.
explanation.walkthrough: A nightmare was once thought to be a witch or demon riding the sleeper, so a tormented sleeper was ridden by a hag.
explanation.definitionFit: Tormented or oppressed, originally by bad dreams thought to be caused by a witch sitting on the sleeper.

clue.text: Fattening up-ready for the tax inspector's kill ?

definitions.text: Fattening up-ready for the tax inspector's kill ?

parts.words: Fattening up-ready for the tax inspector's kill ?
parts.note: fattening an animal for slaughter becomes filling out paperwork, forms the tax official will use against you

explanation.surface: A farmer fattens his beast for slaughter, the taxman watching.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about livestock being fattened, but the 'filling' is done to official forms, completing tax returns that give the inspector his prey.
explanation.definitionFit: Completing official paperwork, such as tax returns, is called filling in forms.

clue.text: It has teeth that can be made to chatter

indicators.note: can be made to means the letters of the next word can be reformed into the answer

explanation.surface: Something toothed that rattles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'teeth that can be made to chatter' suggests a cold person, but 'chatter' rearranged gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a toothed wheel or bar that a pawl engages so it turns only one way.

clue.text: The last thing to hit

parts.note: to 'hit the sack' or its synonym with dried grass means to go to bed, the final act of the day

explanation.surface: The final target before stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit' suggests striking something, but the idiom 'hit the ___' means go to bed, the last thing one does each day.
explanation.definitionFit: Going to bed is called hitting the dried-grass bedding in the idiom, done last thing at night.

clue.text: " The bird of night did sit, — and shrieking" (J Caesar)

definitions.text: " The bird of night did sit, — and shrieking" (J Caesar)

parts.words: " The bird of night did sit, — and shrieking" (J Caesar)
parts.note: Casca in Julius Caesar describes an owl sitting at noon in the market-place, crying out, as an omen

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the blank from Julius Caesar, Act 1 Scene 3: the owl sat in the market-place calling out and shrieking, an ill omen.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry of an owl, the bird of night, is its characteristic call.

clue.text: Rough kind of life, starting from scratch ?

definitions.text: Rough kind of life, starting from scratch ?

parts.words: Rough kind of life, starting from scratch ?
parts.note: a quarrelsome life is named after two animals that fight, and the scratch is the first animal's weapon

explanation.surface: A hard existence begun with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from scratch' usually means from nothing, but here it means beginning with a scratch, as a fight between household pets does.
explanation.definitionFit: A life of constant quarrelling is likened to the endless fights of two traditionally hostile pets.

clue.text: Polish premier ?

parts.note: Polish is read as 'Pole-ish', relating to a pole of the earth, and premier as a British prime minister

explanation.surface: The prime minister of Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' suggests Poland, but it means of the Pole; Lord North was British prime minister from 1770 to 1782, during the American War of Independence.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord North was a British prime minister whose title is also the direction of the upper pole.

clue.text: In which bad performers were often clapped

definitions.text: In which bad performers were often clapped

parts.words: In which bad performers were often clapped
parts.note: clapped means put into fetters, not applauded, and bad performers are wrongdoers

explanation.surface: Poor actors who were nevertheless applauded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clapped' suggests applause for a performer, but criminals were 'clapped in' shackles.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetters and shackles made of metal were used to restrain prisoners.

clue.text: These can be made from this piece of paper

definitions.text: These can be made from this piece of paper

parts.words: These can be made from this piece of paper
parts.note: the first word of the clue is a rearrangement of the five letters of the piece of paper

explanation.surface: Things that can be fashioned from a page.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests origami, but 'These' is literally made by rearranging the letters of the word for a piece of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A single rectangular piece of paper is a leaf of standard size.

clue.text: Take what is left, to succeed

explanation.surface: Accept the remainder in order to win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to succeed' means to follow on as heir, not to win.
explanation.definitionFit: Heirs receive property left in a will, and an heir succeeds to a title or estate.

clue.text: This timer is deceptive

parts.note: put the number before 'timer' to make the word for a cheating, unfaithful lover

explanation.surface: A clock that cannot be trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timer' suggests a clock, but adding the number in front makes a two-timer, someone unfaithful to a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-timer deceives a partner by seeing someone else, so the number completes the word for cheat.

clue.text: The man who let the sands run out in former days ?

definitions.text: The man who let the sands run out

explanation.surface: The figure who let the hourglass empty long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Time is pictured with an hourglass, letting its sands run; the hyphenated adjective describes things belonging to the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Time, an aged figure carrying an hourglass, personifies passing years; old-fashioned things belong to former days.

clue.text: Nick's record' score

explanation.surface: Nick holds the high score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick's' looks like a man's name with a possessive, but it is 'nick is', a small cut; the 's is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small V-shaped cut is a nick, and a tally mark cut on a stick records a score.

clue.text: The roving variety of bag.

indicators.note: a variety of something is another version of it, so the letters appear in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: The wandering type of travel case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roving' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder with 'The'; 'variety of' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: A small case packed for a single night away is called an overnight bag, or simply an overnight.
